newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thailand takes Moody's rating review in stride.
newsitem.headline: Thailand takes Moody's rating review in stride.

text.p: Thailand put up a brave face on a decision by Moody's Investors Service to review the country's sovereign ratings, saying it would furnish the U.S. agency with updated information on its improving economy.

Finance Minister Amnuay Viravan said during a weekend economic seminar that investors and financial analysts should not take hasty bearish views on Thailand after Moody's announced on Friday that it might cut Thailand's A2 long-term foreign currency debt and deposit ratings.
Moody's said its review was prompted by concerns over the soundness of Thailand's financial sector as well as by constraints on macro-economic policy-making.

"Thailand will move to clarify its position...Standard and Poor's still retains its strong credit ratings for Thailand and remains confident in its stability. Standard and Poor's is a world respected agency," Amnuay told reporters.
Standard and Poor's said on Friday it had no plans to downgrade Thailand.
Amnuay, voicing confidence in Thai fiscal and government debt financing positions, called on analysts to give separate assessments of sovereign and private sector debts.
He said although U.S. government debt enjoyed high market ratings, the U.S. market also traded low-quality junk bonds floated by its private sector.
Finance ministry officials said the Thai government and state enterprises had a solid record of meeting all debt obligations.
They said despite Moody's decision, the Thai government would proceed with its plan to float $500 million, 10-30 year Yankee bonds in March.

Moody's, which last September downgraded Thailand's short- term debt rating to P2 from P1, said it also put on review the current A2 long-term foreign currency ratings of Bangkok Bank, Thai Farmers Bank, Siam Commercial Bank, Industrial Finance Corp of Thailand and Export-Import Bank of Thailand.

Sirichai Sakornratanakul, executive vice-president of IFCT, attributed Moody's decision to recent market pressure faced by the Thai baht and an interest payment default by property developer Somprasong Land Plc on its Euro-convertible debentures early this month.
"Moody's based its review largely by looking at outdated information," he said.

The baht has depreciated sharply against a surging dollar in the past two months and speculators have mounted sporadic attacks on the currency on rumours that Thailand might devalue the baht to help boost exports and narrow the current account deficit.

Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh said on Saturday he would not blame Moody's for its action, although he believed the rating company might not have access to full and accurate information on Thailand.

"We should not panic. Thais should be serious in belt-tightening...our (austerity) policy will be followed up by consistent actions. We should stop being wasteful and avoid over-stretching economic growth," he said.
Chavalit said he knew the identities of four speculators who had spread rumours of a possible baht devaluation and warned that he would take action against them.
